title: Effect of Top‑k Filtering on Token Probabilities
body:
Consider five tokens with raw softmax scores 39, 53, 24, 51, and 40. Converting to percentages gives the full distribution shown on the left.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full vs Top‑3 Renormalized Probabilities","caption":"Top‑3 tokens keep 69.56% of total probability; their shares are renormalized.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["t1","t2","t3","t4","t5"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[18.84,25.6,11.59,24.64,19.32]},{"label":"Top‑3 renorm.","values":[0,37,0,35,28]}],"variables":[{"name":"full","role":"input","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"k","role":"input","type":"int","min":1,"max":7,"value":3},{"name":"renormalized","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.1.values"},{"name":"keptShare","role":"result","type":"float","min":1,"max":100,"value":69.56}]}}
```

Top‑k keeps the highest‑scoring tokens—in this case the three with scores 53, 51, and 40—so they retain 69.56% of the total mass.

The remaining probability is discarded and the kept values are renormalized, producing the right‑hand bars.

title: Top-k filtering and reported token probabilities
body:
When a language model generates text, top-k filtering drops any token outside the top $k$ candidates before sampling. The remaining probabilities are then rescaled to sum to one.

Look at the bar heights in the chart to see how the distribution shifts.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-4 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 90% of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under","by","in"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[31,22,17,20,10]},{"label":"Top-k renormalized","values":[35,24,19,22,0]}],"variables":[{"name":"full","role":"input","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"k","role":"input","type":"int","min":1,"max":5,"value":4},{"name":"renormalized","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.1.values"},{"name":"keptShare","role":"result","type":"float","min":1,"max":100,"value":90}]}}
```

Because the dropped tokens remove probability mass, dividing by the kept share increases the relative weight of the surviving tokens. Thus, the reported probability of the chosen token changes after renormalization.

title: Top-k filtering and token probabilities
body:
Top-k filtering restricts token sampling to the $k$ most likely candidates from a language model's output distribution. This operation discards any token outside the top set by setting its probability to zero.

To ensure valid sampling, the remaining probabilities are renormalized so they sum to one. Look at the group comparison in the chart to see how individual token values change.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-3 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 75% of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under","by","in"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[20,30,25,10,15]},{"label":"Top-? renormalized","values":[27,40,33,0,0]}],"variables":[{"name":"full","role":"input","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"k","role":"input","type":"int","min":1,"max":7,"value":3},{"name":"renormalized","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.1.values"},{"name":"keptShare","role":"result","type":"float","min":1,"max":100,"value":75}]}}
```

When these probabilities are renormalized, every kept token receives a higher relative share than it had in the original softmax distribution.

The reported probability of the chosen token is thus scaled up by the inverse of the kept share sum.

title: Top-k Filtering and Token Probabilities
body:
Yes, top-k filtering alters the reported probability of a chosen token because it discards unlikely candidates and rescales the remaining probabilities.

When generating text, a model computes a raw probability distribution across all vocabulary tokens using the softmax function.

Notice how the bars change between the full distribution and the renormalized set in the chart.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Full softmax and top-4 sampling","caption":"The kept tokens originally hold 90% of the probability. Divide each kept probability by that total.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"%","variant":"grouped","categories":["on","near","under","by","in"],"series":[{"label":"Full softmax","values":[40,10,20,15,15]},{"label":"Top-? renormalized","values":[44,0,22,17,17]}],"variables":[{"name":"full","role":"input","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"k","role":"input","type":"int","min":1,"max":7,"value":4},{"name":"renormalized","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":100,"at":"series.1.values"},{"name":"keptShare","role":"result","type":"float","min":1,"max":100,"value":90}]}}
```

Applying top-k filtering sets all probabilities outside the top $k$ entries to zero.

To ensure the remaining values sum to one, the framework divides each surviving probability by the sum of the kept subset's original shares.

title: Comparing Multiclass Predictions
body:
Softmax functions turn raw model scores into normalized probabilities across multiple classes.

By applying the exponential function to each score and dividing by the sum, they ensure all outputs range between zero and one and sum to $1$.

When evaluating two different predictions, we compare their respective probability vectors side by side.

Look for the contrasting dominant class distributions between the two inputs in the grouped bar chart below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Two softmax probability vectors","caption":"Illustrative values; compare categories on the shared scale.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["Cat","Dog","Bird"],"series":[{"label":"Input A","values":[0.61,0.06,0.33]},{"label":"Input B","values":[0.36,0.46,0.18]}],"variables":[{"name":"weightsA","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[54,5,29]},{"name":"weightsB","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[39,50,20]},{"name":"probabilitiesA","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"probabilitiesB","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.1.values"}]}}
```

Input A strongly favors the first class with a probability of 0.61, while Input B shifts preference to the second class at 0.46.

title: Comparing Softmax Probabilities
body:
Softmax turns raw model scores into probabilities by exponentiating and normalizing them. This lets us directly compare two multiclass predictions across shared categories.

Look at how each model assigns confidence across categories in the grouped bars.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Two softmax probability vectors","caption":"Illustrative values; compare categories on the shared scale.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["Cat","Dog","Bird"],"series":[{"label":"Input A","values":[0.58,0.21,0.21]},{"label":"Input B","values":[0.4,0.49,0.11]}],"variables":[{"name":"weightsA","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[58,21,21]},{"name":"weightsB","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[40,49,11]},{"name":"probabilitiesA","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"probabilitiesB","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.1.values"}]}}
```

Input A strongly favors the first class with probability $0.58$, while Input B splits its highest weight at $0.49$ for the second class.

Because the outputs sum to $1$, comparing them reveals relative confidence shifts between different predictions.

title: Comparing Multiclass Softmax Probabilities
body:
When a model makes multiclass predictions, it outputs raw scores called logits for each available category.

These raw scores can vary widely and lack bounds, making direct comparison across different models or inputs difficult.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Two softmax probability vectors","caption":"Illustrative values; compare categories on the shared scale.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["Cat","Dog","Bird"],"series":[{"label":"Input A","values":[0.66,0.08,0.26]},{"label":"Input B","values":[0.06,0.51,0.43]}],"variables":[{"name":"weightsA","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[55,7,22]},{"name":"weightsB","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[6,54,46]},{"name":"probabilitiesA","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"probabilitiesB","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.1.values"}]}}
```

The softmax function converts these raw logits into normalized probabilities by exponentiating each score and dividing by the sum across all classes.

Look at the grouped bars to see how input A assigns the highest share to the first category while input B peaks on the second.

This transformation ensures that all output values range between $0$ and $1$ and sum to exactly $1$ across the categories.

prompt: How do softmax probabilities compare two multiclass predictions?
title: Comparing Multiclass Softmax Predictions
body:
Softmax converts raw model scores called logits into normalized probabilities that sum to one across all target classes.

When comparing two multiclass predictions, the function exponentiates each logit and divides it by the sum of all exponentiated values.

Look for the contrasting probability distributions between the confident model and the uncertain model in the chart below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Two softmax probability vectors","caption":"Illustrative values; compare categories on the shared scale.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["Cat","Dog","Bird"],"series":[{"label":"Input A","values":[0.34,0.39,0.27]},{"label":"Input B","values":[0.31,0.39,0.3]}],"variables":[{"name":"weightsA","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[39,44,30]},{"name":"weightsB","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[18,23,18]},{"name":"probabilitiesA","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"probabilitiesB","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.1.values"}]}}
```

Input A shows a sharp peak where one class dominates with a probability of 0.70, indicating high model confidence.

Input B shows nearly uniform probabilities near 0.33 across categories, reflecting high uncertainty or ambiguity in the prediction.

prompt: How do softmax probabilities compare two multiclass predictions?
title: Comparing Softmax Probabilities
body:
Softmax functions turn raw scores into normalized probabilities across multiple classes by exponentiation and scaling. For instance, classification models output real-valued logits for each possible class label.

Notice how the grouped bars display the probability distribution shifts between two different input sets across shared categories.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Two softmax probability vectors","caption":"Illustrative values; compare categories on the shared scale.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["Cat","Dog","Bird"],"series":[{"label":"Input A","values":[0.08,0.48,0.44]},{"label":"Input B","values":[0.09,0.55,0.36]}],"variables":[{"name":"weightsA","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[6,35,32]},{"name":"weightsB","role":"input","type":"float","min":1,"max":1000,"value":[7,45,29]},{"name":"probabilitiesA","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.0.values"},{"name":"probabilitiesB","role":"result","type":"float","min":0,"max":1,"at":"series.1.values"}]}}
```

By exponentiating each logit, the softmax operation ensures all resulting values are positive and sum to exactly one. This makes it straightforward to compare predictions from different models side by side.

When comparing predictions, the highest probability indicates the predicted class for each input.
